en: Regarding the *Fahua jing lun shuji* (Commentary on the Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) and the *Miaofa lianhua jing youbotishe* (Upadeśa on the Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma): "Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma" is the original title of the sūtra being explained;
"Upadeśa" is the name for the treatise that explains it. The essential meaning of the sūtra being explained has two parts: first, the opening...
The gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*). Second, the manifestation of the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). As for "true reality," it refers to the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*).
As for the "gate of skillful means," it refers to the path of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*). These two paths both possess the profound principle of the timing and method [of practice];

therefore, they are called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*). Regarding the term "lotus," it serves as a metaphor to reveal the Sublime Dharma, which emerges from the turbidity of the ten types of pride and unfolds its petals.
This is the reality of that vehicle; therefore, it is likened to a lotus flower. Furthermore, the lotus flower serves as a metaphor to specifically manifest the qualities of the Dharma.
Within this sutra, both the provisional means (*upāya*) and the ultimate truth (*bhūtatathatā*) each have two aspects: namely, the Dharma and the person.

"Dharma" refers to the qualities of the sublime Dharma (*saddharma*), which is named "sublime Dharma" based on its essential nature. "Person" refers to the qualities of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka*), which are manifested through metaphorical illustration.
"Indication" (śāsana) is named "Lotus"; its meaning is as explained above. *Upadeśa* is named "Discourse" (*vāda*).
It refers to the principle of discourse among the twelve divisions of the scriptures. It is also called *mātṛkā*. The term *le-ga* is an abbreviation of the sound.
Because it explains the scriptural texts of the Vinaya and investigates profound meanings, it is named *upadeśa*. Based on...
Because it establishes the name of the treatise based on the sūtra it explains, this is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Alternatively, within this treatise, the essential meanings contained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are subsumed under the term "Treasury" (*pitaka*). Paramārtha translated [the name] as Tianqin (Devasharma);

that person was originally the younger brother of a celestial deity, hence he was named Tianqin. The śramaṇa Xuanzang translated it as Shiqin (Vasubandhu), for the Bodhisattva took birth in the world.
Because he prayed to the deity of Vasubandhu, it was named accordingly. There are two versions of this treatise:
one translated by Ratnamati, which lacks the verse of homage; the other translated by Bodhiruci, which includes the verse of homage.
The wording differs slightly, but the meaning is no different. What is now explained is the translation by Paramārtha.
Within the introductory homage, there are three main sections; the first verse offers general reverence to the Triple Gem and expresses the aspiration to explain the intent of the sutra.
The next verse specifically pays homage to the Teacher and addresses the assembly, clarifying the purpose of composing this treatise. The subsequent one and a half verses consist of:

first, a general dedication to the supreme conditions, requesting that they grant their protective care; and second, "prostration," which means to arouse a pure mind, transform it into a fruit of love, and prostrate with the entire body.
"The ocean of perfect enlightenment" refers to the Buddha’s bodhi, which is vast, profound, of a single flavor, and endowed with all virtues.
It is called the Ocean of Perfect Enlightenment. Regarding "pure dharmas," this refers to the teachings realized; because they are all free from defilement and supreme, they are termed "pure dharmas.
Regarding the "unconditioned Saṃgha," this refers to the assembly of noble ones (ārya); because they share the same name as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called the "unconditioned Saṃgha.

In its most eminent sense, this refers exclusively to Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*). The latter two phrases clarify the intended meaning of the sūtra. Furthermore, it may also be interpreted as follows:

Regarding the manifestation of reverence through performing prostrations to the Three Jewels: for what purpose is this done? It is for the sake of those with profound wisdom and those with sharp faculties, in order to reveal the *vyākaraṇa* (explanatory discourse).

"Those with profound wisdom" refers to those who have turned toward Bodhi; that is, the Śrāvakas who have attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) because they have realized the nature of the dharmadhātu.
"Those with sharp faculties" refers to Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and proceed directly toward Bodhi, rather than [following the path of the Śrāvakas].

Because of these detours, for the sake of these two types of people, the One Vehicle Dharma is taught. "Opening" (kai) means to teach directly and open [the way]; "showing" (shi) means to indicate through detailed exposition.

Furthermore, "opening" refers to opening up the provisional (expedient means), while "showing" refers to showing the ultimate. When the teaching is complete and the principle is perfect, it is called the *vyañjana-śāstra* (the treatise of phonemes).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says regarding the elder instructing his son: first he uses the "half-syllables," and later the *vyañjana*. This refers to...
The meaning is similar. In that sutra, the "half-syllables" (*ardhākṣara*) are a metaphor for the Hīnayāna, while the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna.
What is called the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise? At the time when the kalpa was first formed, Maheśvara gave it to Viśvakarman.
Through the union [of parents], a son was born named Brahmā. He had four faces; he taught the four Vedas. On the single head atop his crown, he taught one Veda.
That which was spoken from the four faces all pertains to worldly matters, whereas that spoken from the crown is profound and difficult to understand.
Of what is practiced in the world, there are only the four Vedas; later generations further composed six types of treatises to explain these four.
The *Piṭaka* and the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra* constitute one of the six treatises (*ṣat-śāstra*). The *Aṭṭha-piṭaka* explains the principles of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*).

As for the *Aṭṭha-piṭaka*, it is that which will be discussed later. The Westerners (Indians) value this science of grammar so highly that it takes twelve years to achieve a thorough understanding; it is not something that can be mastered by a beginner or a venerable elder alone.
Therefore, *viga* is used as a metaphor for the Mahāyāna. As for *jigyan munim*, it means to appropriately revere the Honored One, the Muni.
Although within the preceding homage to the Buddha there was a general salutation, because he is the Teacher of the Doctrine, he must be revered separately.
"And the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas" refers to Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Śāriputra, and others who were present to respond to the teaching.
Although one previously prostrated to the Saṃgha as a whole with six types of prostrations, because this is a specific response to the assembly, it is necessary to pay special respect.

The following two lines indicate that the composition of the treatise is complete. Furthermore, these two [lines] demonstrate the purpose for which the teachings are set forth: the desire to cause oneself and others to [realize] the Dharma.
For the sake of benefit, this abbreviated version of the *Sūtra* and the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* has been produced.
*Mātṛkā* means "matrix" (*mūla*), because it can clearly reveal the hidden meanings of the source, just as a matrix is the source of letters.
It should properly be called *Mātṛkā*, but here it is abbreviated and thus termed the *Lakṣaṇa-śāstra*. Hereafter, may protection be granted, as stated in the text.
It should be understood that the preceding section on the respectful preface is now concluded.

From here on follows the formal exposition of the sūtra text, which constitutes the main body of this treatise. If one were to categorize the sūtra text according to this treatise, it is divided into three major sections.
The first is the "Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching," which consists of the accomplishment of seven kinds of merit.

The first is the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta). The second is the "Fivefold Division" (*pañcavastuka*), which breaks down into two parts: the "Clarification of the One" and the "Opening of the Expedient Means" (*upāya*);

the latter begins with the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*). The third is the "Division of Counteracting the Ten Unsurpassed [Views] to Reveal the True Reality" (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*);

this extends from the "Parable" chapter (*Aupamya-parivarta*) until the end of the sutra. As for the "Division of Dissemination," it is subsumed within the "Tenth Unsurpassed" and therefore is not established separately. Thus it is explained.
In the first chapter, the first two sections are cited first. Regarding the fact that not all of the *paryāya* section of the sūtra is cited:

because its wording is obscure and difficult to understand, it is cited and then explained; whereas [the parts where] the characteristics are manifest and easy to know are all included in the summary.

Although "Thus have I heard" and so forth are not explained individually, because the text is brief, they are cited together with the sūtra. As for the phrase "I take refuge," etc., the one who compiled the sūtra, intending to...
In order to bring forth this sutra, one first takes refuge. It is logically appropriate for all sutras to contain this;
where it is absent, it has been omitted for brevity. The treatise says: This first chapter of the introductory section demonstrates the accomplishment of seven kinds of merit.
What are these seven? First, the accomplishment of the introduction (*nidāna*); second, the accomplishment of the assembly (*parṣad*); third, the Tathāgata’s intention to preach the Dharma.
1. The accomplishment of the arrival of the proper time; 2. The accomplishment of abiding in accordance with the majestic deportment (īryāpatha) as taught in the Dharma;
3. The accomplishment of the reliance on the causes for teaching; 4. The accomplishment of the assembly’s presence and desire to hear;
5. The accomplishment of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s response.
The commentary states: In the treatise’s exposition of the sutra, there are two parts: first, the enumeration of the topical headings; second, the detailed explanation of those headings.

Within the first part, there is first a general opening and subsequently a specific enumeration. Regarding the initial general opening, the phrase "this dharma-gate" refers to the dharma-gate of the entire work as a whole.
The phrase "the first chapter" refers specifically to the very first chapter among the twenty-eight chapters.
The initial statement would have sufficed; why, then, does it further say "the first chapter"? This is to clarify that the twenty-eight chapters are condensed into three divisions.
Now, this introductory chapter (Nidāna-parivarta) belongs to the first division and is the first chapter; thus, it possesses both meanings.
Regarding the statement "the first and foremost": the accomplishment of the seven kinds of merit refers to the seven matters, beginning with the introduction (*nidāna*).

Whether taken collectively or individually as appropriate, each possesses the function of generating faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), thereby assisting in the manifestation of the merit of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is established as follows.
It cannot be destroyed; for this reason, it is called the "accomplishment of merit. In the section on individual enumeration, there is first an inquiry followed by a listing.

Regarding the accomplishment of the introduction (*nidāna*): the five phrases beginning with "Thus have I heard" contain few words and characters, and furthermore, they constitute the general introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*).
Therefore, these are collectively termed the "introduction. Regarding the accomplishment of the assembly (*parṣat*): according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is also...

The six phrases of the "Certainty of Faith" (*śraddhā-prasāda*) included in the introduction (*nidāna*) constitute the general introduction (*sāmānya-nidāna*). Therefore, they are set aside here to focus on the specific meaning.

This is termed the "Accomplishment of the Assembly" (*parṣat-sampad*), because it concerns the capacity of the disciples (*vineya*) for whom the teaching is intended; since the excellence of the teacher’s motivation is paramount, the depth of the teaching must be revealed by way of the superior or inferior nature of those disciples.
The *Gayāśīrṣa-śāstra* likewise uses the term "Section on the Accomplishment of Disciples Who Should Hear [the Teaching]" with the same underlying intent. This is for the following reason:
This is because it also possesses the meaning of a general introduction (*pūrvayoga*). First, the scriptural text is cited; this is cited together with the introduction.

Regarding the phrase "when the Tathāgata desired to preach the Dharma, the time had arrived for its accomplishment": although more than forty years had passed since his attainment of enlightenment, he had never yet preached this wondrous Dharma.

This was because the faculties of sentient beings were not yet mature and the time for preaching had not yet arrived. Now that their capacities have matured, the time for preaching the Dharma has come.
The time has arrived; therefore, he first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* as a preliminary introduction to this present sūtra.

Regarding the phrase "abiding in the accomplishment of conduct in accordance with the Dharma taught": since the time for preaching had arrived and he was about to begin his discourse, he acted accordingly.
One must necessarily abide in accordance with the Dharma and conform to dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*), because the Dharma taught by the Buddha is held in the highest reverence;

it is only after considering the place and the assembly that he arises to teach. This is the protocol for teaching the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; therefore, it is called "abiding in accordance with the Dharma and conforming to dignified decorum.
Regarding the accomplishment of the causes for relying on the teaching: having already established oneself in conformity with decorum, flowers rain down and the earth trembles.
The ground [of the teaching] serves to manifest internal realization. Furthermore, he emits a magnificent radiance, and the assembly beholds this rare omen;
they all give rise to a longing and yearning mind. Because the teaching is delivered based upon this desire, it is called the "cause for teaching based on reliance.

As for the great assembly desiring to hear the accomplishment of the Dharma discourse, although they previously wished to inquire, the signs had not yet appeared; thus, they spoke to urge [the Buddha].
Question: Because the characteristics of desire are about to manifest, it is called "the manifestation of the desire to hear.

Mañjuśrī’s response is termed "accomplishment" because he directly perceives the characteristics of past causes and effects; by articulating the doubts of the assembly, he is able to resolve their obstructions, and thus it is called his "accomplished response.
Although all seven types of matters possess the significance of sequential order, they are categorized here according to their general names.

This is for the sake of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta). However, the first part receives its name from its general application, while the remaining six parts all establish their titles based on specific meanings, just as there is no contradiction in naming the five sense objects "objects" (artha).

The Commentary says: Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of the introductory section (*nidāna*), one should understand that within this Dharma-gate two kinds of supreme accomplishments are manifested.
What are these two? First, the manifestation of the accomplishment of the most supreme meaning among all Dharma-gates;
second, the manifestation of the accomplishment of the meaning of sovereign qualities (*vaśitā-guṇa*). This is like the city of Rājagṛha, which is superior to all others.
All other cities and dwellings, as well as Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, are surpassed by all other mountains; this is because it reveals that this *dharmaparyāya* possesses the most supreme meaning.
As the Sūtra says: "The Bhagavat was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain."
The commentary states: The following section provides an exegesis according to the text. Within the exegesis of the introductory section (*nidāna*), only the dwelling place is explained;

the rest are omitted for brevity, as their textual meaning is identical to that of other sūtras and lacks any distinct significance. This section contains four parts: first, the summary statement reiterating the chapter title;

second, the inquiry into the number followed by their individual enumeration; third, the indication of specific matters to clarify the meaning; and fourth, the citation of the sūtra text to reaffirm the point. It says: "Furthermore, the introductory section is completed."

"Regarding 'as for' (jù): this refers to the restatement of the chapter title. The dwelling place included in the introductory section (*nidāna*) does not merely serve as the physical basis for the arising of the teaching;

it also possesses a specific symbolic meaning. It is explained in order to manifest that distinct meaning. Furthermore, the phrase 'this dharma-gate' below serves as a general heading for the supreme truth (*paramārtha*).
Because the meaning it symbolizes is profound, it is exhorted that one 'should know. As for the question 'What are the two?': this refers to the subtle number. First..."
From the words "The above" onwards, the specific enumeration of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) is presented.

To demonstrate that it is the most supreme accomplishment among all dharma-gates means that its wondrous dharma-qualities realize the profound; for it is the most supreme meaning among all dharmas. Its scriptural transmission (*āgama*) is profound;
for it is the most supreme meaning among all gates. Why is it supreme? Because it is the vehicle upon which all Buddhas ride to the ultimate.
Because it is the vehicle. Since there is no other superior dharma beyond this, the accomplishment of the meaning of sovereign merit refers to the merit of the Dharma-preacher.
The former is the vehicle upon which one rides; this is the person who rides it.

Just as he has realized for himself, he explains and bestows it upon others without depending on further deliberation, thereby accomplishing the task to be done; thus it is called the accomplishment of sovereign merit.
As stated below regarding Rājagṛha: pointing to a specific instance to clarify the meaning, it is superior to all other cities and dwellings.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Some say that among the four directions of Jambudvīpa, the east is the beginning because it is where the sun first rises.
Among the lands of the eastern direction, the kingdom of Magadha is the most excellent. Within the kingdom of Magadha, the city of Rājagṛha is the finest.
In that city there are twelve hundred million households; the people therein are for the most part intelligent, widely learned, and possessed of great knowledge.

That country is prosperous and joyful; alms are easily obtained. Situated amidst mountains, it contains many secluded and tranquil monasteries, and thus those who practice seated meditation delight in dwelling there, as explained in detail in the treatises.
Now, seeking the meaning, there are seven kinds of excellence: first, excellence of name, because it is called Rājagṛha (King’s House);
second, excellence of direction, because it is located in the east; third, excellence of location, because there are many households; fourth, excellence of inhabitants...
First, it is superior in having many wise people. Second, it is superior in abundant joy, as alms-food is easily obtained.
Third, it is superior in seclusion, being situated among the mountains. Fourth, it is superior in dwellings, as there are many monasteries. This Dharma-gate is likewise so:

it is the king among all sutras, the most excellent among Dharma-gates, extensively encompassing all vehicles, the abode of the wise, and richly endowed with the joy of the Dharma. It resides in Jambudvīpa.
"Mountain. Regarding "the place where the noble and holy ones delight to dwell," and "Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain being superior to all other mountains," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further states:
Question: There are four other mountains, such as Vaibhāra, Vepulla, and so forth. Why do [the Buddhas] dwell most frequently on Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain?
Answer: Because Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain is the most excellent among the five. How is it the most excellent? Because of its vihāra (monastery).
It is near the city, yet the mountain is difficult to ascend. Because it is difficult to ascend, worldly people do not come; because it is near the city, one does not grow weary of seeking alms.
One who realizes this dharma-gate likewise does not abandon the world to enter nirvana, but enters both samsara and nirvana.
Prajñā is unstained by the world, yet it does not abandon the world; Great Compassion constantly receives all beings.
To say that this dharma is manifested by means of the most supreme meaning is to manifest its establishment as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The rest is as in the text.
The Treatise says: Regarding the accomplishment of the assembly, there are four kinds of meanings by which this accomplishment is manifested;
these should be understood. What are the four? First, the accomplishment of number; second, the accomplishment of practice; third, the accomplishment of the inclusion of meritorious qualities;
and fourth, the accomplishment of abiding in accordance with the Dharma through dignified deportment.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, the "Explanation of the Achievement of the Assembly. Within the sutra text, there are two parts: first, the enumeration of the names and numbers of the fifteen assemblies;
second, a general manifestation of the fourfold assembly’s dignified conduct as they abide in accordance with the Dharma.

In the preceding portion, citing from the sutra, two assemblies are first enumerated: namely, the assembly of bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas. Within these two assemblies, the text contains five sections.
First, the indication of the category; second, the chanting of the number; third, the praise of virtues; fourth, the enumeration of names; fifth, the summary.

In the commentary, following the citation of the sūtra, the latter two [sections] are retained as they appear in the *Vibhāṣā*, while within the exegesis, they are collectively reduced to four parts. Within these, there are three: first, the indication; second, the enumeration; third, the explanation.
Regarding the "fourfold," the number is indicated. Under the heading "What are... and so forth, their names are enumerated. As for "the accomplishment of the number":
This collectively reveals the number of vows for the fifteen assemblies. Regarding the "accomplishment of practice," this collectively reveals all the karmic practices possessed by these assemblies.
As for this accomplishment of practice, there is the meaning but no explicit textual passage;

furthermore, names such as "bhikṣu" or "bodhisattva" may themselves signify their respective practices, as general and specific names are established according to their individual modes of action. Regarding the "accomplishment of the inclusion of merit," this collectively...
This reveals all the merits possessed by this assembly. While the text explicitly mentions the community of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, its meaning extends to the other assemblies as well;

it is simply that the text is concise. Regarding "those who abide in the accomplishment of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) according to the Dharma," this generally reveals the dignified conduct possessed by this entire assembly.
These four types of meanings are categorized according to their respective significance; it is not the case that every single description of an assembly contains all four. First, and...

Fifth: In all the textual passages of the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the four [aspects] are complete. As for the remaining thirteen textual passages, they possess only two [aspects], namely number and deportment;
however, their meaning universally encompasses all four, as each, according to its respective application, also possesses the aspect of conduct and virtue.
The Treatise says: Regarding the accomplishment of number, it refers to the fact that the great assembly is incalculable. Regarding the accomplishment of practice, there are four kinds:
first, the śrāvakas who cultivate the practices of the Hīnayāna; second, the bodhisattvas who cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna;
third, those bodhisattvas who, possessing mastery over supernormal powers, manifest at will and are able to cultivate the Mahāyāna, such as Bhadrika... [and so forth].
The sixteen virtuous men, such as Dravya and others, are fully endowed with the inconceivable deeds of a bodhisattva and constantly manifest in various forms and appearances,
namely as upāsakas, upāsikās, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs. The fourth category refers to the renunciant śrāvakas,
whose deportment is fixed and who thus differ from the bodhisattvas.
The commentary states: From here on follows the detailed explanation. "The great assembly is innumerable" generally indicates fifteen types of sentient beings, as their number is immeasurable.

Within the explanation of the accomplishment of practice, there are four [sections]: the first two reveal the internal practices cultivated within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, while the latter two reveal the external conduct manifested within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. In reality, there are these four kinds.
All [these practices] are common to both the householders and the renunciants. However, within the fourth [category], only renunciants are mentioned because their characteristics are more manifest.

To weary of and renounce birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), to abandon the task of transforming others, and to swiftly seek one's own liberation by cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth, is called the practice of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Although they weary of birth-and-death, they do not abandon sentient beings; for the sake of universal salvation, they cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
These are called the practices of the Mahāyāna. These two are termed the internal practices cultivated within. Once the internal practices are perfected, external manifestations also appear.
The Bodhisattva manifests before the fourfold assembly according to conditions; the Śrāvaka, being fixed in one way, mostly manifests as a renunciant.
These two are termed the external practices manifested outwardly.
The Commentary states: "All are Arhats," and so forth, consists of sixteen phrases that manifest the accomplishment of the śrāvaka’s merit;
therefore, they are all non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "And so forth" consists of thirteen phrases that manifest the accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s merit.

The commentary states: From here below, the third [section], the accomplishment of the inclusion of merits, is explained. Within this, first the merits of the two assemblies are indicated, and subsequently the merits of the two assemblies are explained.
The reason that the topical headings are not explicitly cited in the indication is merely that the text follows a style of brevity.
The Commentary states: Regarding the accomplishment of the qualities of the śrāvakas, one should understand that these sixteen phrases demonstrate the meaning as subsumed under three categories.

The explanation is as follows: within the exposition, first the qualities of the śrāvakas are explained, and subsequently the qualities of the bodhisattvas are explained. [Regarding] the qualities of the śrāvakas...
Regarding the virtues, there are three parts: first, opening the three gates; second, enumerating the three gates; and third, explaining the sixteen phrases based upon the three gates.

This [section] constitutes the opening of the gates; that is to say, those sixteen phrases—beginning with "all are arhats" and so forth—are to be understood as manifesting the general meaning of the virtues through the three gates of "superior-to-superior arising" and the rest.

The treatise says: What are the three gates? First, the gate of successive arising; second, the gate of general and specific characteristics; third, the gate of the inclusion of matters. The commentary explains:

Regarding the gate of successive arising, it refers to the relationship between the accomplished and the means of accomplishment based on the phrases; that is, upon the phrases of the means of accomplishment, [the accomplished]...

Regarding "successive arising" (*uttarottara-pravṛtti*): it is so called because that which is established arises upon the sentence that establishes it, or because that which establishes arises upon the sentence that is to be established;
thus, it is named "successive arising. Here, "arising" (*pravṛtti*) means "establishment" (*siddhi*). Regarding the "gate of general and specific characteristics" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-mukha*):

based on the principle of stating a heading and then explaining it, one first presents a single general statement and subsequently explains it with specific statements; hence it is called the gate of general and specific characteristics. This concludes the summary.
Regarding the "gate of grasping phenomena" (*vastu-saṃgraha-mukha*): it is based on complete and incomplete phrases. If it is a complete phrase, a single phrase encompasses all virtuous phenomena.
If it is an incomplete phrase, two or three phrases are combined to encompass all virtuous phenomena; therefore, it is called the "gate of grasping phenomena."
The Treatise says: Regarding the gate of the "superlative arising," it refers to those for whom all [defilements] have been fulfilled and exhausted; thus they are called Arhats.

(Omitted) As for "reaching the foremost shore," it is because they have properly attained right knowledge and liberation of mind, and have properly attained various meritorious qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), and so forth.
The commentary states: From here below, the explanation proceeds according to the gates. This specifically follows the first gate, the "Arising from the Uppermost," for its explanation.

Within this first gate, there are ten examples: (1) arising from what follows; (2) arising from two preceding instances; (3) arising from both preceding and following instances; (4) arising from the text; (5) arising from the meaning;
(6) arising from both text and meaning; (7) arising by immediate succession; (8) arising by skipping over; (9) ... [and so forth].
"Arising alone," "arising ten times again," and "because all outflows are exhausted, one is called an Arhat"—these have four categories:
first, arising subsequently; second, arising according to the text; third, arising in immediate succession; and fourth, arising alone.
These meanings can be understood through reasoning. An Arhat is so named because they are worthy (arhat) and because they receive the sublime offerings of the world. Furthermore...
He is called a "slayer of thieves," for he has forever destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

He is also called "unborn," for he shall never again undergo birth within the realms of conditioned existence (*pratisaṃdhi-jāti*). These three meanings all arise because his outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted.
By the exhaustion of all outflows, he becomes an Arhat; because he has attained mastery over the mind, he is termed "one whose outflows are exhausted. This...
There are four types of arising: first, arising subsequent to [a preceding state]; second, arising from the text; third, arising with an interval; and fourth, arising independently.
Because it is never bound to the various afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "mastery of mind. If the mind were not masterful, the outflows (*āsrava*) would be difficult to exhaust.
Therefore, by attaining mastery of the mind, one achieves the exhaustion of all outflows. As for what are called "the outflows," they refer to—
The "outflows of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*) and so forth refer to the three types of outflows. As stated in the *Niniju-hyakuju-kyō* (Sūtra on Ninety-nine or One Hundred [Outflows]):
"All afflictions (*kleśa*) bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), with the sole exception of ignorance (*avidyā*), are designated as the outflow of desire.

All afflictions bound to both the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), with the sole exception of ignorance, are designated as the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*). If sentient beings have either not yet abandoned desire or have already..."

He is free from desire. He has eliminated all the heterodox, perverse, and deluded discriminations of the various non-Buddhist paths—those evil views born of ignorance that shroud the mind—and he does not, based on such evil views, seek after some aspects of those desires while becoming detached from other aspects.
Up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, all ignorance pertaining to those three realms is subsumed as one and termed the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Because there are no further afflictions, it is said that "the mind has attained mastery.

Because one has well attained the liberation of the mind and well attained the liberation through wisdom, one is called "one who has attained mastery of the mind. This also consists of four [aspects].
For example: first, arising before and after; second, arising by way of the text; third, arising in succession; and fourth, arising repeatedly. Why does it arise repeatedly?
Because the mind possesses both general and specific mastery. "General" means it is not subject to the various afflictions (*kleśa*);
"specific" means it is liberated from the two kinds of bonds. One who has well attained liberation of mind is free from craving for the three realms.

Therefore, one who has rightly attained liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) has already abandoned all defiled ignorance (*avidyā*). As it is said: "Through the abandonment of craving, the mind attains liberation;
through the abandonment of ignorance, wisdom attains liberation. In response to the question regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it is answered:

"Because one is separated from all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, the mind attains liberation. Why? The Buddha said: "When one is separated from defiled attachment, the mind attains liberation."

[Question: What is liberation? [Answer: It is because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) binds and confines; since the mind possesses great power, for this reason it is said that there are no other afflictions [besides it].
When craving is severed, the others are also severed. Furthermore, all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) belong to either craving or views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Afflictions belonging to craving obscure the mind, while afflictions belonging to views obscure wisdom. Because one is detached from craving, the fetters belonging to craving are also abandoned, and one attains the mind of liberation.

Liberation occurs because of being free from ignorance (*avidyā*). It belongs to the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); furthermore, one attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā*). This is the dharma of non-retrogression;

because one attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), it is called "well-attained. Because one is far removed from the capacity for seeing [the object], it is called "one who has no further afflictions" (*niḥkleśa*).
This is the cause arising uniquely by way of meaning, which possesses three types: first, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Second, objects that accord with craving and so forth; third, those not yet destroyed by the eye. For now, we shall speak of two types of "seers":

namely, those who see through improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), and those who see objects that accord with craving and so forth. Because they have distanced themselves from both of these causes, [they do not see].
The afflictions that were to be abandoned no longer arise in the world, because he has attained liberation of mind through wholesome [attainment] and liberation through wholesome wisdom;
therefore, he is called one whose mind is well-tamed. This also consists of four examples, meaning they arise in succession following the preceding text.
When one is not free from craving and the like, the mind is not disciplined; because one is able to be free from them, the mind is well-disciplined.
Thus, through the three liberations, one achieves the well-disciplined mind. Regarding the three explanations of the Buddha-ground, there is one interpretation:

those in training (śaikṣa) are free from the one hundred and twelve kinds of conceptualization and heavy afflictions (*dausthulya*) to be abandoned by insight; because they are no longer unruly, they are like fine horses.

It is called "well-tamed. According to one interpretation, because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are free from the one hundred and twenty-eight kinds of afflictions abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation, they are not rigid or stubborn;
thus, like genuine gold, they are called "well-tamed. According to the true meaning, all these belong to the lineage that is dedicated to enlightenment (*bodhi-gotra*).
They are entirely capable of producing great fruits and turn according to the Buddha’s intention, just as [gold is malleable].
Because he is wise and intelligent, he is called "tamed" (*dānta*); what is now termed "subdued" (*vinīta*) has the same meaning.

If one speaks only of being "subdued," it applies generally to all three senses [of taming]. If one says "well-tamed" (*suvinita*), it refers only to the latter two senses, for although those in training (*śaikṣa*) are subdued, they are not well-tamed.
Regarding the phrase "great dragon among men": traversing the various evil paths is like walking upon level ground.
"Roads that are free from obstruction; having already traversed what was to be traversed and having already reached what was to be reached.

This refers to the various evil realms (durgati) arising through their respective causes, namely the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*), because they are defiled and thus to be loathed and feared.
"Level roads" refers to the truths of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-satya*), because they are pure and thus to be rejoiced in. By means of emptiness...
Practicing with equanimity, one contemplates their lack of intrinsic nature; thus, although one traverses the path of affliction, there is no attachment.

Therefore, it is said to be like a level road, free from all obstruction. Furthermore, because one knows suffering and abandons its origin, one traverses the various evil paths as if they were a level road.

Being free from all constraints and hindrances, one realizes cessation and cultivates the path; thus, what was to be practiced has been practiced, what was to be reached has been reached, and what was to be done has been done.
These are the Great Dragons among men who have attained the antidote and have subdued the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is the introduction to the preceding text, further established by its meaning: namely, that within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), suffering has already...

He knows: "Origination has been abandoned; cessation has been realized; the path has been cultivated. One who knows thus has performed what was to be done, for he has accomplished what was to be accomplished by the former Great Nāgas.
Furthermore, because he knows that the cause of origination is exhausted, it is said that he has attained the antidote and has conquered the enemy that is the afflictions (kleśa).
Thus, one who has completed what was to be done will not be born again hereafter. As it is said:

"Because the corresponding task has already been accomplished" is an explanation of the meaning. This means that within the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the fruit of suffering does not arise;

regarding the knowledge of suffering and so forth, one no longer acts further. Therefore, it is said that "it will not arise again later," just as when a corresponding task has already been accomplished.
"Having laid down all heavy burdens" means that what was to be done has been done, and what was to be performed has been completed.
"To take up a heavy burden in future lives" and "having already abandoned it"—these constitute a redundancy in the phrasing. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are coarse and heavy, and they constantly afflict; therefore, they are called a 'burden. As the Buddha said: 'What is the burden? The five aggregates are the burden.
Because causes are exhausted and effects do not arise, one is able to abandon the heavy burden of the five aggregates; therefore, this should be so understood."
This constitutes the accomplishment of what is to be done. Among those who have laid down their burdens and performed what was to be done, they have realized cessation and cultivated the path;

this is because it does not mean that the burden has not been laid down. To explain further: since the burden of future rebirth has already been cast off, a sutra states: "One who has discarded the burden yet is capable of bearing a burden.

This means that one has discarded the burden of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), while being capable of bearing the burden of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga*). Having attained this...
"Having attained one's own benefit" means that one has already laid down the heavy burden and realized *nirvāṇa*. This is the independent meaning of the text.
Because the burden of the aggregates (*skandha*) is not one's own benefit, yet one is able to lay it down; and because *nirvāṇa* is one's own benefit, yet one is able to realize it.
Therefore, it is said: "Having attained one's own benefit and exhausted all fetters of existence.
Regarding the phrase "having attained one's own benefit and severed the causes of all afflictions," this also arises as an independent textual meaning.

Because one has attained the benefit of *nirvāṇa*, one can exhaust all states of existence (*bhava*); because one has severed the causes of all afflictions (*kleśa*), one can exhaust all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and afflictions.
As for the "cause," it refers to the seer, the seen, improper reflection, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because one who has properly attained right knowledge and liberation of mind as previously described has exhausted all outflows," this is an instance where a single textual element is separated by an intervening passage.
This means that because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, one has attained right knowledge and liberation of mind; it is not merely by seeing a physical form that one attains liberation.
For example, when the disciple of the brahmin Makkhali took his teacher’s corpse, placed it upon a bed, and carried it through the city, he proclaimed in crowded places:
"If anyone looks upon Makkhali the butcher with anger, they shall all attain [liberation]."
"The path of purity—how much more so for those who prostrate and make offerings. Many people believed these words.
When the bhikṣus heard this statement, they addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is the meaning of this? The Buddha spoke in verse: "An inferior person seeks purity with his own eyes;
Such is the ignorant and unreal path. With all fetters and afflictions filling the mind, How can he see with his eyes?"
One perceives the Path of Purity (*viśuddhi-mārga*). If one could perceive purity through the eye, what need would there be for the jewels of wisdom and merit?
It is through wisdom and merit that purity is attained; there is no such thing as seeking purity through the eye.

For those who have attained mastery over all minds by virtue of their skillful knowledge of the wisdom of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), this [realization] arises solely through the meaning [of these paths] regarding seeing and cultivation.
The Path can be personally realized and known; it is not brought about through the guidance of another's teaching, and for this reason it is called "sovereignty.
The *Gayāśīrṣa-śāstra* states that the meaning is the same for one who practices according to the teachings based on non-perversion:

because they well know and see the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and because they well know and practice the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) based on non-perversion. Through these two causes, one practices according to the teachings.
Therefore, one attains mastery over all minds. What was previously called "mastery over the mind" refers to the sense of not being subject to afflictions (*kleśa*).
This statement, "attaining mastery over all minds," refers to the sense of realizing and knowing all the noble paths (*āryamārga*).

"Those who have reached the first shore" refers to those who have properly attained right knowledge and liberation of mind, and who have properly attained various merits such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the *anāsrava-samādhi*. This is the meaning of the passage taken independently.

For two reasons, they are said to have "reached the first shore": first, because they differ from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*); second, because they have properly attained right [knowledge].
Because of the liberation of the mind, there is a second type: liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).

There is no separate cultivation of meritorious qualities, because one has already well attained such qualities as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the pure samādhis. Regarding the sixteen phrases explained above, they can be categorized into three groups according to their characteristics.
First, those that are solely accomplished results rather than means of accomplishment; these consist of five phrases, namely: the mind of an Arhat...
Well-tamed; having exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*); having attained mastery over all minds; having reached the supreme further shore.

Two [of these] are only the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and not that which is accomplished (*sādhya*); these consist of two phrases, namely: "well-attained liberation of mind" (*ceto-vimukti*) and "well-attained liberation by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*).

Three are both the means of accomplishment and that which is accomplished; these refer to the remaining nine phrases. As for those that are neither the means of accomplishment nor that which is accomplished, there are none.
The summary verse says:
The textual meanings of the preceding and following sections, Whether adjacent or single and double, Are formed through the mutual interaction of subject and object;
One should know that the arising of these superior meanings Consists of one, seven, three, five, and ten, With the last being exclusively that which is accomplished.
Five or six [factors] can only establish [the status of a "person of renown"], while the remaining nine apply to both meanings.
The Treatise says: Regarding "Mahā-arhat" and so forth, it is because they have attained mastery over the mind and reached the other shore (pāramitā). ... (omitted) ...
for this reason, they are called "those known by the multitude."
The commentary states: Based on the three gates, the explanation of the sixteen [aspects] has concluded with the first gate.
Therefore, following this, the concluding text is now explained. As the text listing the names is easy to understand, it is omitted here without further explanation.
The Commentary states: Regarding the section on general and specific characteristics, all [of these] consist of sixteen phrases concerning the Arhats and so forth.

The first phrase is the general [characteristic], while the remaining phrases are specific. (Omitting intermediate text... Fifteenth: One should know as it truly is that the various beings born together attain all merits for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which explains the sixteen phrases according to the method of general and specific categories.

Regarding the designation "Arhat" as "one who is worthy" (*arhan*): although the name "Arhat" contains three meanings, it is here termed "general" based on the meaning of "worthiness," because this applies to all fifteen types of worthiness.
As for these fifteen types, they are distinguished within the general category of worthiness according to their respective meanings.

Detailed Enumeration. First, "because one should receive offerings of food, drink, bedding, seats, honor, and respect": this means that one should receive offerings because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted;

one should receive worldly offerings of food and drink and so forth, and should lead the great assembly to teach and transform all beings, meaning that one should teach and transform them because there are no further afflictions (*kleśa*). One should...
The first [task] is to transform and teach the great assembly. The second is that one should enter [the world], because one should attain mastery of the mind;
thus, one may enter villages and so forth, wandering without fault. The third is that one should subdue others, because one should attain liberation of mind through goodness;
thus, one should subdue non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the like. As Nāgārjuna said: "All non-Buddhists..."
And so forth. If the factors that assist the path (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are not fulfilled, whether one practices all virtues or practices two specific merits, one will be unable to attain the Way.
It is like a person who seeks purity through giving alone; there are those who claim that purity is attained merely through giving and observing the precepts.
There are those who claim that purity is attained through giving alone or through meditative concentration alone;
there are those who claim that purity is attained through wisdom alone. Such various paths are incomplete. They speak of purity based on either no merit at all or only slight merit.
Although the minds of such persons are liberated in one respect, it is not called a "good liberation" or *nirvāṇa*, because it is not complete.
As it is said: a person without merit cannot cross the great ocean of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
a person of minor merit cannot cross the path of the Dharma of the Good Way. This refers to the matter of the brahmin Subhadra as spoken of by the Buddha regarding crossing over.

The full explanation should be understood as follows. Regarding the fifth [point], one should observe it: because one should attain liberation through wisdom by means of skillfulness, one should swiftly observe phenomena with wisdom.
One who observes swiftly is able to enter deeply into the meaning; one who enters deeply is able to practice extensively.
Because it is said that [the Dharma] is swift; one should preach the Dharma as the sixth duty.

Because one should well-subdue the mind, one should preach the Dharma neither too quickly nor too slowly, in accordance with the Dharma, and without weariness. Seventh, one should practice *dhūta* (ascetic purification).
Because one should be like a great dragon among men, one should sit in quietude in secluded places and the like; for the nature of a dragon delights in stillness and possesses few desires.

And so forth. As in the Vinaya regarding the story of the bhikṣu practicing dhyāna who requested the dragon’s pearl: the eighth [requirement] is that one should practice wholesome conduct, because one must perform what ought to be performed;

thus, one practices exclusively in goodness and does not become attached to the various dhyanas. The ninth is that one should practice the noble conduct of emptiness, because one has already accomplished what was to be done;
thus, one should practice the conduct of emptiness, for apart from the wisdom of emptiness and non-self, there is nothing further to be done.
Because it is difficult to discern. Tenth, one should practice the noble path of signlessness (*animitta-caryā*), because one should abandon the burden of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Within *nirvāṇa*, one practices the path of signlessness. Eleventh, one should practice the noble path of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-caryā*), because one should attain the benefit of *nirvāṇa*.
Within the three realms (*tridhātu*), one practices the path of wishlessness. Twelfth, one should subdue...
Regarding worldly dhyāna: because one must exhaust all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*), one is able to subdue the pure mind of worldly dhyāna. Thirteenth:
one should give rise to the supreme merits of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because one must skillfully attain the liberation of the mind through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
It is able to give rise to the supreme merit of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Fourteenth is the supreme merit of the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
because one should attain mastery over all minds and because one possesses the knowledge of the path of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, one is able to realize this supreme merit.
Fifteenth is the supreme merit of knowing, as it truly is, those beings born together with oneself; because one has reached the ultimate...
Because they have reached the other shore, they are able to know, as it truly is, the merits attained by the assembly of those born together with them.

This "assembly of those born together" does not refer to the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), but rather to the assembly of noble ones (*ārya*). This is further threefold, sequentially demonstrating their wisdom, abandonment, and beneficent virtue.
The Commentary states: Regarding the "door of encompassing matters," these fifteen phrases encompass ten kinds of merit.
(Omitted) Tenth is the "encompassment of the foremost merit," as stated in the Sūtra: "Because one has reached the foremost shore."
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which explains the sixteen phrases according to the gate of the matter of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*).
Regarding the statement that these fifteen phrases above "gather ten kinds of merit," this indicates that their gathering is explained solely in terms of the distinct [categories]. Thus it says:
"The fifteen demonstrate the fruits that can be expressed and the fruits that cannot be expressed. This is because conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) are termed "expressible."
Regarding the fruit: because there are distinctions in their characteristics, conditioned meritorious qualities are called "expressible fruits.

Because there are no such distinctions in their characteristics, unconditioned meritorious qualities are called "inexpressible fruits. The *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* states: "From this point onward, one need no longer cultivate the nature of the objects of practice.
Having truly severed all afflictions, at that very moment, regarding the cessation of all afflictions, [one abides in] nirvāṇa."
Regarding overweening pride (*adhimāna*): because one has distanced oneself from overweening pride, one truly experiences that there exists this ultimate clarity and liberation (*vidyā-vimukti*).
Having attained clarity and liberation, one understands the nature of the objective sphere (*gocara*) of what has been attained.

Because one has thereby emerged from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it should be known that clarity and liberation also constitute an emergence; within nirvāṇa, they are capable of apprehending [it].
The two kinds of designations for the grasped object are both non-existent, because all conceptual proliferation has been eternally extinguished and abandoned.
Therefore, even regarding all conditioned phenomena, one may engage in successive questioning and answering concerning the designations of the grasper and the grasped.

Regarding the distinctions of discourse: within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of ultimate *nirvāṇa*, all questions and answers, as well as all distinctions of discourse, are entirely unreasonable.
Among the ten [results], the first is the result that is inexpressible; the remaining nine are all results that are expressible.
As for "virtue" (*guṇa*), it refers to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); its essential nature is virtue itself, being without the differentiation of marks.

Therefore, in terms of their essential nature, they are called virtues (*guṇa*) and meritorious qualities (*guṇa*). Regarding "various meritorious qualities" (*nānā-guṇa*): this refers to the qualities of subduing others;
because they differ according to what is subdued, they are termed "various. Regarding "non-contradictory meritorious qualities" (*avirodha-guṇa*): these are the qualities of self-conformity;

because one is able to conform oneself [to them], they are called "non-contradictory. Regarding "supreme meritorious qualities" (*viśeṣa-guṇa*): because they possess great power, they are called "supreme" meritorious qualities. As Nāgārjuna said:
It is said that among the countless arhats, he is called a "dragon-elephant" (nāga-hastin) because of his supreme power.
This is because among those who move through water, the dragon’s power is great, while among those who move on land, the elephant’s power is great.

Furthermore, he is like a great dragon king who emerges from the great ocean, raises vast clouds that completely cover the void, emits great flashes of lightning that illuminate heaven and earth, and pours down a great rain of nectar that moistens all things.

It benefits all things. All the *ārya* categories are likewise. From the great ocean waters of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), clouds of compassion and mercy arise, moistening those who may be saved.
It manifests great radiance and various transformations, preaching the Dharma of true reality (*tathatā*).
It rains upon the minds of disciples, causing the sprouts of goodness to emerge. For those who should perform supreme meritorious deeds, it provides offerings as follows:

"Coming forth" and so on are termed "that which ought to be done. Being the foremost among offerings made according to the Dharma, it is termed "the excellence of what ought to be done. Regarding the "one whose merit is fulfilled":

because that which was to be accomplished during the stage of training has already been fulfilled. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One attains the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*)."

The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) are therefore called "that which is to be done. The acquisition of the various untainted roots of goodness, such as the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), is therefore called "that which has been accomplished.

The attainment of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is therefore called "that which is to be done," while the attainment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is therefore called "that which has been accomplished.

The attainment of the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) is therefore called "that which is to be done," while the attainment of the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) is therefore called "that which has been accomplished. First.
Among the seven surpassments of merit, "surpassing craving" means that within this [practice], craving is regarded as a heavy burden.
"Surpassing the pursuit of life, offerings, and honor" means that because one has attained the benefit of nirvāṇa, one is able to surpass worldly pursuits such as the desire for life and so forth;
for through the pursuit of life and the like, one does not achieve one's own true benefit. The treatise asks: what is one's own benefit, and what is not one's own benefit?
Practicing all wholesome dharmas is called one's own benefit; all other dharmas are called what is not one's own benefit.

Because virtues such as faith, ethical discipline, relinquishment, concentration, and wisdom are superior to all worldly wealth and treasures, because they constantly bring happiness in both this life and future lives, and because they enable one to reach the city of ambrosia (*amṛta*), they are called one's own benefit; the rest are not one's own benefit. As a verse says: "In this world..."
They give rise to various unwholesome dharmas and are no different from birds and beasts.

One should constantly seek the essential path of right wisdom to attain liberation from old age and death and enter nirvana. Those who transcend the upper and lower realms do so because they have exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhava*).

There are three [existences], namely the three existences such as the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth. "Fetters" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the nine fetters, such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth. The treatise states:

"The exhaustion of these fetters and existences, and the exhaustion of existences and fetters, is therefore called the 'exhaustion of the fetters of existence' (*bhava-saṃyojana-kṣaya*). It is like a person falling from a high place."
When a person on the stage of "not yet arrived" dies, even if they have not yet died, they know they will certainly die;
likewise, these Arhats, whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) are already exhausted, know that what remains must necessarily be exhausted, and thus it is said that their fetters are exhausted.

Regarding those of the highest and highest merit, it is because they possess the quality of immovability (*akopyadharman*). As for those who should perform the merit of benefiting sentient beings, it is because they have attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Because they penetrate the immeasurable and so forth. Regarding the "preeminent qualities," this is because they have reached the ultimate.

As for the passage listing their names, the treatise has omitted details. The concluding passage has already been explained as before. Within the fifth section, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, there are likewise five parts:
first, the designation of the assembly; second, the proclamation of the number; third, the praise of their virtues; fourth, the listing of their names; and fifth, the summary conclusion.
The Treatise says: Regarding the accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s merits, those thirteen phrases should be understood as manifesting the meaning through two categories.
What are these two categories? First, the category of the upper and lower branches; second, the category of the inclusion of matters.

The commentary states: From this point downward, the text reveals the gate of the Bodhisattva’s inclusion of meritorious qualities; this constitutes the third section, the passage praising these virtues.

Within this, there are three parts: first, the citation of the chapter title; second, the classification of the gates; and third, the explanation of the meaning. This [current section] consists of the citation of the chapter title and the classification of the gates.
Within this, there are three further divisions: first, the classification; second, the inquiry; and third, the enumeration, as found in the text.
The Treatise says: Regarding the "upper and lower branches," this refers to the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*);

this meaning should be understood. The commentary explains: The general characteristic constitutes the thesis statement (*uddiṣṭa-pada*), and is therefore called the "upper branch. The specific characteristic constitutes the explanatory statement (*nirdeśa-pada*), and is thus called the "lower branch.
The phrase "all [of whom] do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" is the thesis statement.
All [the verses] obtain the twelve phrases, such as the *dhāraṇī* and so forth; this is because they are the explanation of those phrases. Fourth, for what reason?
Within the praise of the Bodhisattva’s virtues, he explains those merits using only two gates and does not speak of the gate of "successively arising superiorities.

What is the meaning of this? The answer is: within the virtues of the Śrāvaka, one praises the virtues of those in the same stage; the subject and object mutually support one another, thereby establishing existence.
"Arising from the highest of the high. This "arising from the highest of the high" demonstrates the meaning of the mutual completion of subject and object.
Therefore, within the Bodhisattva’s praise of virtues, the merits of the three specific stages are clarified; thus, there is no meaning of the mutual completion of subject and object.
For this reason, the gate of "arising from the highest of the high" is not taught [in that context]. Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the opposite of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Its essence is the fruit of Buddhahood, which consists of five factors:

namely, the pure phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*) and the four categories of wisdom (*jñāna*). Because both wisdom and the locus of wisdom are called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*), and because enlightenment is also the abandonment [of afflictions], all are termed "enlightenment.
As for "non-retrogression," it is so called because one does not regress due to possessing the ten causes listed below; thus, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, one is able to...
Non-retrogression means that one will certainly realize [the goal] and advances in cultivation moment by moment; this is called non-retrogression.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one advances spontaneously and never retreats from the cultivation of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), because there are no afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, one is not moved by any effort involving signs (*nimitta*); this is called non-retrogression. For these reasons, the eighth stage is named "Non-retrogression."
The sign of the shaking of the earth: because afflictions cannot move it. There are four kinds of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression of faith.

This refers to the sixth stage of the ten faiths, called the "mind of non-retrogression," because from this point onward one no longer retrogresses into false views. Second, non-retrogression of position.

The seventh of the ten stages is named the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). It is so called because from this point onward, one does not retrogress by entering the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Third is non-retrogression in realization: because the dharmas realized from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward are never lost. Fourth is non-retrogression in practice:

because from the eighth stage upward, one is able to cultivate both conditioned and unconditioned dharmas. Since this bodhisattva is now at or above the eighth stage, [he is established in these three types of non-retrogression].
Regarding the statement "non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi": it is called non-retrogression because one is certain to realize it.
The Upādhyāya said: there are five kinds of bodhi. First is the bodhi of the initial resolve (*cittotpāda-bodhi*); this refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
If one has not yet attained it, retrogression occurs up until the sixth mind; once the sixth mind is attained, there is no further retrogression regarding those dharmas not yet attained.

Having departed, one has already attained non-retrogression; yet regarding dharmas not yet attained, there is still the possibility of retrogression and loss. Second is the bodhi of subduing the mind:

this refers to the stage of the three worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*), where one has not yet attained [the higher stages]; from the ten understandings (*daśa-vyākhyāna*) up to the seventh dwelling (*saptama-vihāra*), regarding dharmas both unattained and already attained, there is retrogression and loss in all cases.
From the seventh dwelling onward, regarding dharmas already attained, there is no retrogression; regarding those not yet attained, there is still retrogression. Ten.
Regarding the dedication, from the sixth dedication onward, one has already attained non-retrogression with respect to both dharmas already acquired and those not yet acquired. Why is this?

It is because the mind is refined through the three types of refinement (*pariṣodhana*). As for "subduing the mind," it means subduing and eliminating the afflictions (*kleśa*) by bringing the mind under control;
that is, practicing the various deeds such as the six perfections (*pāramitā*) and subduing and eliminating the six faults.
Because it subdues such hindrances and so forth, it is called "subduing the mind" (*citta-vinaya*). Third is the "enlightenment of the enlightened mind" (*citta-bodhi*).

This refers to the period from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, during which one has already attained non-retrogression regarding what has been gained, yet still experiences retrogression regarding dharmas not yet attained.

This is because one gives rise to defiled attachment toward what one has already attained, and fails to progress toward the superior dharmas above. Regarding the "retrogression of the enlightened mind" within the attainment of what is to come: first—

Having already attained illumination within the stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes the true principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); therefore, it is called the Bodhi of the Illuminating Mind. Regarding the Bodhi of the Path of Emergence:

this refers to the dharmas of the three stages from the eighth stage upward. Because they flow spontaneously within the "swift current," there is no retrogression regarding dharmas already attained or yet to be attained.
As for "emergence from the path": one has already emerged from the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*) and ascended.
Because it is *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), it is called the "path leading out. As for the five unsurpassed bodhis, these are the fruit of Buddhahood. Question:
What characteristics should one say characterize a Bodhisattva who has already entered the eighth stage (*bhūmi*)? Answer:

One should say that because they have attained spontaneous engagement through mental attention toward the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), which is without applied effort (*anābhoga*) and without purposeful activity (*anabhisamskāra*), they are without fluctuation regarding any signs.
Having attained mastery, they dwell on the ground of purity. What are the characteristics of a bodhisattva who has entered the ninth stage? Answer:
It should be said that because they have attained mastery over the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*);

and because they have attained faultless, immeasurable, and vast wisdom; and because they have attained vast and unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), they are able to gladden all sentient beings.
Because of the mind, he is called a Great Dharma Master. Question: What characteristics should one say a Bodhisattva who has entered the tenth stage possesses? Answer:
One should say that he has attained the same great empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as all Tathāgatas; that he has attained the great Dharma-body like a cloud;
and that he has attained all great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). He is named a Tathāgata. He is non-retrogressive and manifests ten kinds [of signs].
Both of these meanings should be understood.
From this point onward, based on the section concerning the lower members (*adhara-aṅga*), the text is cited and its meaning explained. Master Ji said: "Within the section on the lower members..."
There are twelve phrases, which are manifested through ten types. Within these ten types, they are divided into two categories:

the first nine concern self-benefit, and the last one concerns benefiting others. The first nine are further divided into two: the first eight are conditioned virtues (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*), and the last one is unconditioned virtue (*asaṃskṛta-guṇa*).

Within the former [the conditioned virtues], there are again two: the first five are merit and wisdom (*puṇya-prajñā*), and the latter three are compassion and wisdom (*karuṇā-prajñā*). Abiding in the hearing of the Dharma...
They all attained *dhāraṇī*. *Dhāraṇī* is here translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*). There are two types of total retention:
first, gathering; second, dispersing. Gathering means to hold. This refers to "retention through hearing": hearing the words and their meanings, and maintaining them without forgetting.
To be able to retain what one has heard is called "comprehension" (saṃgraha). Hearing is the essence of *dhāraṇī*, which consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are able to endure, reflect upon, and cultivate all dharmas."
That treatise explains as follows: "Able" refers to the wisdom of hearing; "reflection" refers to the wisdom of contemplation;

and "retention" refers to the wisdom of cultivation, because these three functions are distinguished within the single wisdom of cultivation. "Dispensing" means giving, for one bestows the four kinds of *dhāraṇī* upon sentient beings.
Second, "non-retrogression in joyful exposition" refers to the eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna*). Eloquence is precisely the four types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Seventh is eloquence (*pratibhāna*), because of the joy of speaking. Regarding the four types of eloquence, these are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):

first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*). These two, respectively, are the unimpeded wisdom that understands the teachings and their underlying principles.

Third is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which is the unimpeded wisdom that understands all regional dialects and sounds. Fourth is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), which is...
The wisdom that is unimpeded in preaching the Dharma and so forth, and the meaning of the sevenfold eloquence, are as explained extensively elsewhere.
Regarding the three explanations of non-retrogression, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated: "There are three kinds of wheels of Dharma. First is the wheel of turning [the Dharma]:

this refers to when the Buddha, on the eighth day of the second month, attained enlightenment; and on the eighth day of the fourth month, he went to Vārāṇasī and turned the Wheel of the Four Truths for the five bhikṣus."

First is the Wheel of the Truth (*satyadharmacakra*). Second is the Wheel of Illumination (*ālokadharmacakra*), which refers to the period after the Buddha’s enlightenment, during the seventh year, when he went to the banks of the Śubhavastuka River—three *li* from the Jetavana Grove—and taught the non-characteristic Mahāyāna, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*;
this is called the second wheel of the Dharma. Third is the Wheel of Sustenance (*dhāraṇadharmacakra*), [occurring] during the thirty-eighth year after the Buddha’s enlightenment.

Later, at the Dharma Hall of the Ghost King of Vaiśālī, for the sake of Bodhisattvas such as Paramārthasamudgata, he taught the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other such scriptures—namely, the definitive Mahāyāna teachings. This is called the third turning of the wheel of Dharma. The first was the Hīnayāna;
the second was the Mahāyāna; and the last is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which universally subsumes the three vehicles and brings them all back to the Mahāyāna.
These three, in their respective order, are named Turning, Illuminating, and Sustaining. These three names are established based on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

According to this interpretation, among those in the Mahāyāna who have not yet turned away from the Hīnayāna, they enter the second wheel of Dharma; those who have already turned away from the Hīnayāna enter the third wheel of Dharma.
Question: If that is so, why does the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* state that those whose nature is inclined toward tranquility will ultimately never...?

[The opponent] asks: "Furthermore, it is said that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is a statement of intentional meaning (saṃdhāyabhāṣita). How can it be considered the third wheel of Dharma? [The respondent] answers:

"That which says they are destined for the nature of tranquility (śama-dhātu) and cannot attain great enlightenment (mahābodhi) was spoken with reference to the time before they had turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]."

If they turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] at that time, it is not that they cannot achieve [enlightenment]. Question: If this is so, how does this differ from those śrāvakas who redirect their aspirations? Answer:

Those who previously generated the mind for Great Awakening but subsequently regressed and remained in the Lesser Vehicle, yet re-enter the Mahāyāna within the single dispensation of Śākyamuni, are called "śrāvakas who redirect their aspirations.
Therefore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) states that these are called "those who have regressed from Bodhi."
The *Sūtra* refers to the subsequent stage and thus calls it "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*); the *Śāstra* refers to the initial stage and thus calls it "regressive mind.

Therefore, we know that those who once regressed but later returned are called "śrāvakas dedicated to bodhi. As for those who have never previously resolved their minds [for awakening], [they are not so called].

In Śākyamuni’s single dispensation, because their faculties have not yet matured, they ultimately do not enter the Great Vehicle. Due to their adherence to the Dharma of the ignorant, they give rise to the notion of final nirvāṇa;
such persons are called *śrāvakas who incline toward quiescence*. In the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, they are termed "definitive śrāvakas.
Because they cannot be turned back within a single dispensation, those persons necessarily give rise to the notion of final nirvāṇa; therefore, they are named "those who incline toward quiescence."
Because they are unable to turn their minds away from the Hīnayāna, it is also termed "definitive.
