The determination of the *Āgama* regarding the mind is likewise so. As for "present desire," it refers to the arising of a thought of something unprecedented within one's own internal mind;
because it is also said that [the object] appears within [the mind], it is called "present desire. As for "non-present desire," it is as follows:
Only within one's own internal mind does the thought of something unprecedented arise; because it does not manifest externally, it is said that there is no manifestation of desire.

Possessing these four virtues, one is a fit vessel for hearing the Dharma. Regarding the fourth point, proper conduct according to the rules, and the fifth point, the basis for the teaching, among these two categories there is only the manifestation of desire; however, in this sixth category, all [four] are fully present.
The two types of desire—those present and those not present—are called the "accomplishment of the desire to hear before the great assembly.
This section consists of two parts: first, the citation of the chapter title; second, the explanation beginning with the question addressed to a single person.
In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there are two sections: first, the expression of doubt; second, Maitreya’s formal inquiry. Here, both of these are explained in full.
Furthermore, within the "Great Root" (Mahāmūla) doubts, there are two: first, the doubt of Mañjuśrī; second, the doubt of the great assembly.
Here, we shall explain only the doubt of Mañjuśrī and not that of the great assembly. As for the question addressed to a single person, the intent of the question is this:
why is it that only Mañjuśrī is questioned and no one else? This is said because when many people wish to hear [the teaching], a sense of wonder arises. This...
This is the answer. Since many people wished to hear Mañjuśrī’s response, the reason for questioning Mañjuśrī alone was to conclude the intent of the inquiry.
[Objection: The great assembly did not know that Mañjuśrī was the one capable of answering;
how then can it be said that many wish to hear Mañjuśrī’s response? [Response: Maitreya is able to know this.
The karmic conditions of the great assembly depend upon Mañjuśrī; for if they hear what Mañjuśrī speaks, they will inevitably give rise to a sense of the marvelous.
Such a manifestation shows that the disciples of the World-Honored One accord with the Dharma and do not remain far from it—this explains the intent behind Mañjuśrī’s ability to answer.
Nevertheless, even Maitreya, whose rank is perfected as the one who succeeds to the position [of Buddhahood], was ultimately unable to know [the answer].
The meaning behind the manifestation of these auspicious omens can only be known by the Buddha. When the Buddha enters samādhi, it cannot be heard [by others]. Only Mañjuśrī is the Buddha;
however, he manifests as such today for the sake of the ten thousand disciples of the World-Honored One. As another sutra states: "In the past, he was the teacher of capable men;
now, he acts as a disciple. This is because the two honored ones do not manifest together. "I am a bodhisattva, following..."

"Conforming to the Dharma and not being in contradiction" has two meanings: first, that he is truly a teacher who demonstrates [the truth] to his disciples, thereby conforming to the Dharma without contradiction;
second, that Mañjuśrī is able to thoroughly comprehend the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Because it does not contradict the Dharma, he is able to answer the questions. Regarding the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifesting the signs of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), this correctly explains Maitreya’s inquiry into the meaning of the intent behind these supernatural transformations.

As for what the significance of these signs is, this explains Maitreya’s doubt, asking by what causes and conditions such an auspicious omen has appeared. "It is for the sake of preaching the Great Dharma" is the Master of the Treatise’s explanation of Maitreya’s [inquiry].

The expression "doubt" is itself the answer. Regarding the manifestation of the great signs: it refers to the light from between his eyebrows illuminating eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction.
"For the sake of preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*" means for the sake of preaching the realization of the profound. Regarding the manifestation of the great auspicious signs:
this refers to the falling of flowers and the shaking of the earth. It is for the sake of preaching the wondrous Dharma attained by the Tathāgata.
The "inconceivable" and so forth refer to the profoundness of the *āgama* (scriptural teaching) by way of its words and phrases.
The Buddha’s emission of light from between his eyebrows refers to the profoundness of realization (*adhigama*).

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is itself the profoundness of realization, the falling of the four kinds of flowers and the sixfold earthquake and so forth serve as auspicious omens for the profoundness of the *āgama*.
Furthermore, that which is "inconceivable in its names and phrases" refers to the profoundness of the Āgamas. It possesses two meanings;
therefore, to look up to and praise Mañjuśrī is to manifest the five contemplations of Mañjuśrī. First, regarding "manifesting all dharmas":
Mañjuśrī is the Buddha, who clearly perceives and manifests all dharmas. Second, "being free from all causes and conditions."
This is because Mañjuśrī does not know through inference or analogy. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"In the case of phenomena perceived directly, causes and conditions have no function; it is solely through the accomplishment of those phenomena within one's own internal mind.

This explains the transcendence of causes and conditions, for Mañjuśrī clearly perceives those phenomena with his own mind and thus does not rely on other causes and conditions. He manifests all manner of...

Regarding the "auspicious signs" (*nimitta*): they are so called because they manifest various specific events. This explains that one must necessarily see these rare signs when interpreting the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, for the events are not singular;
thus, they are termed "extraordinary" (*vicitra*) as they pertain to various matters. As for those signs of events—manifesting, disappearing, abiding, and ceasing—one should understand them well.
"Disappearing" (*astaṃgama*) refers to the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, as well as events such as the erection of stupas and the like.
"Manifest" refers to the various activities of the Buddhas currently existing, such as preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.
"Abiding" refers to the duration of the True Dharma and so forth. "Extinction" refers to the complete disappearance of the True Dharma and so forth.

As for the phrase "because Mañjuśrī is able to explain those matters," this explains the scriptural passage concerning his having already personally approached and made offerings to countless Buddhas of the past.
This is what is meant. Regarding "the accomplishment of what is to be done," this refers to the breaking down of the constructed phenomena of practice.
This has two aspects: first, merit; second, wisdom. These fulfill the internal qualities. Regarding "the accomplishment of the cause," there are two types of causes explained:

first, the direct cause (*hetu*); second, the contributory cause (*pratyaya*). As for the direct cause, it refers to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); by means of omniscience as the cause, one is able to see.
This is because of events from past lives. The accomplishment of causal conditions refers to what are called the "various signs":

the shaking of the earth, the emission of light, and the falling of flowers. Because one saw the Buddhas of past ages manifest these signs and thereby preach the Great Dharma, and now sees Śākyamuni manifest these signs and likewise preach the Great Dharma, these various signs serve as the occasion for preaching the Dharma.

This is the cause. Regarding the accomplishment of the characteristics of the fruit: because of the cause of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the auspicious signs, it is known that he intends to preach the Great Dharma;

thus, this is the fruit consisting of the various characteristics of the Great Dharma. Since Mañjuśrī’s external causes are already fulfilled and his internal virtues are further perfected, he is able to preach just as the Buddha does, for he possesses the fruit of the Dharma. Now, as for the inquiry into the various Buddha-lands, from the above—
Thus concludes the first explanation of Maitreya’s doubts. Now, for the second explanation of Maitreya’s inquiry:
"various and diverse buddha-fields" refers to the eighteen thousand buddha-fields. This demonstrates those within those lands.
Regarding "one should know the various distinctions," there are two intended meanings: first, to demonstrate the various distinctions among the eighteen thousand lands;
second, to demonstrate the distinctions of ten matters within those eighteen thousand lands.
"Pure as the land" explains the scriptural passage: "They all see the adornments of those Buddha-lands. The Tathāgata, for...
Regarding "the foremost": from this point downward, the commentary explains the scriptural text; it does not appear in the standalone sutra. Regarding "the Tathāgata as the foremost":
since the Tathāgata is the sovereign of all sages, he is called the foremost. Regarding "all bodhisattvas and others dwelling in reliance upon the Tathāgata":
this explains the meaning of "foremost. The remaining text is easy to understand. Furthermore, in the manifesting scriptural text, that is also seen.
The passages concerning the Buddhas currently residing in the various lands and so forth do not appear in the single-text version of the sutra.
The *Śāstra* states: "From this point onward, it next clarifies the noble ones, such as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and others."
From this point onward is the seventh section, Mañjuśrī’s response regarding accomplishment. This contains two parts:
first, it clarifies that he is able to respond because he directly perceives the causes and effects of the past; second, it clarifies that he has accomplished ten matters.
Therefore, he was able to answer. This section has two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed sequential explanation.

Within the initial general explanation, "the causal characteristics and resultant characteristics of the past" refers to the events during the time of the twenty thousand Buddhas, beginning with Candrasūryapradīpa.
Regarding "accomplishing the ten matters," "accomplishment" (siddhi) signifies mastery (*vaśitā*) as well as perfection (*paripūrṇa*).
Meaning. Because of the mastery of vision and because of being fully endowed.
Regarding the *Śāstra*’s statement, "How does one directly perceive the characteristics of past causes? and so forth, this is the second section, the specific explanation.
First, it clarifies cause and effect; subsequently, it explains the ten matters. Within the explanation of cause and effect, the phrase "having previously [been] in various Buddha-lands" refers to—
Because there were twenty trillion Sun-and-Moon-Lamp Radiance Buddhas and not just one Buddha, it is said that "those various Buddhas" practiced various deeds in various places;
this explains the characteristics of the cause. During the time of the final Lamp Radiance Buddha, he taught the causes and conditions of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for the sake of all sentient beings.
During the times of the preceding twenty thousand Lamp Radiance Buddhas, they practiced various [deeds].
Regarding the practice: at this time, for the sake of the assembly, he is able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for the characteristics of the fruit:

the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Prabhāpāla), at that time, for the sake of others, preached the fruits obtained from practicing various deeds under twenty thousand Buddhas, which accomplish ten matters.
These are analyzed in four sections: first, citing the names; second, explaining the meanings; third, opening the chapters; and fourth, synthesizing the explanations. First...

First, the enumeration of names, as listed in the text. Regarding the explanation of the meaning: first, "the greatness of the great significance" refers to the greatness of the significance of remembering [the Buddha's] grace;
for the Tathāgata, wishing to expound the Great Dharma, does so through the significance of his great grace.

Second, "the accomplishment of the profound intention behind the worldly words" means that when the Buddha taught the Three Vehicles, there were instances where the words existed but the meaning was not explicit; because the expression was near while the intent was far-reaching, it is termed [profound].
"Profound. Regarding the accomplishment of the rare cause that is directly perceived, the Upādhyāya said:

"For twenty thousand days and nights, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara did not preach the *Lotus Sūtra*, because there were none with the roots for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Only at the time of the final Buddha, Dīpaṃkara, did the roots for the One Vehicle ripen;
thus, he finally preached the *Lotus Sūtra*. Furthermore, it is only now, in the time of Śākyamuni, that the *Lotus Sūtra* is preached; hence [the term] 'profound' is used."
"How rare! Master Jing said: "This Dharma is difficult to encounter even after passing through immeasurable kalpas, for it may not be heard at all;
thus, it is called 'rare. Regarding the four kinds of manifest, supreme, and wondrous [teachings], the Upādhyāya said:

'The twenty thousand Buddhas, such as Candrasūryapradīpa and others, exclusively utilized the Lotus Sutra within themselves for their own enjoyment, and did not preach the Lotus Sutra for the sake of sentient beings.'"
Therefore, it is said to be "supremely sublime. Fifth, regarding the greatness of manifesting and enjoying [the Dharma]:

when the eight princes and others were laypeople, they enjoyed the supremely sublime objects of the five sensory realms; when they left the household life, for eighty minor kalpas, their bodies and minds remained unmoving as they enjoyed the Lotus Sutra.
Sixth, regarding the greatness of manifesting and encompassing the Dharma-wheels of all Buddhas: the Lamp...

7. It clarifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Prabhāpāla) upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and expounded it for eighty minor kalpas for the sake of others.
This is because the causes for the manifestation of the Tathāgata Good Firmness (Sudṛḍha) turning the wheel of Dharma were accomplished;
namely, the eight princes and others who, having received the teachings of Wonderful Light, became firm in bodhi and never regressed. 8. It clarifies the ability [to manifest].
1. The accomplishment of the cause for entering [the path]: This refers to the eight princes and others, because they entered and attained the Buddha-way.
2. The accomplishment of the cause for manifesting recollection: This refers to Maitreya Bodhisattva, who caused [beings] to recollect his former pursuit of fame.
3. The accomplishment of the cause for manifesting the events one has personally undergone: This refers to Mañjuśrī, who manifested his own past...
This is because [the Buddha] passed by the bodies of *Miaoguang* (Sublime Light) and *Mili* (Mañjuśrī), who had formerly sought renown.

These ten are collectively termed "accomplishment through causes" (*hetu-sampad*). "Cause" (*hetu*) has the meaning of "reason" (*so-yi*); "accomplishment" (*sampad*) has the meaning of "mastery" (*zizai*). Master Jing said:
"Accomplishment through causes" refers to Mañjuśrī seeing the ten past events as the answer to the cause of Mili. He saw...
...sovereignty. Therefore, it is said that they are "accomplished. This concludes the third opening chapter; the treatise is clear and explicit, so there is no further need for explanation.
As for the eight great meanings: first, severing doubt; second, increasing and maturing the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*);
third, entering the secret realm of the Śrāvakas; fourth, entering the secret realm of the Bodhisattvas; fifth, advancing toward the supreme purity; sixth, advancing... [text ends]
1. Attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). 2. Establishing the meanings of names, phrases, and chapters. 3. Causing the turning of the wheel of Dharma through realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*).
These eight great meanings correspond respectively to the eight phrases beginning with "desiring the treatise" (*śāstra-icchā*).
Regarding the first, "desiring the great Dharma," what is the great meaning of "wishing to sever doubts"? "Great Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma; that is, the Mahāyāna Dharma.
There are three meanings: first, nature; second, following; and third, attainment. "Nature" refers to suchness (*tathatā*). "Following" refers to wisdom and merit.
"Attainment" refers to the fruit of the four virtues. The first is the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature; the second is the Buddha-nature that is drawn forth;
and the third is the Buddha-nature of the attained fruit. These three Buddha-natures cause one to seek [enlightenment].
The Way consists in generating decisive faith: first, faith that it truly exists, which is the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature;
second, faith that it can be attained, which is the Buddha-nature brought forth; third, faith that there are inexhaustible merits, which is the Buddha-nature realized upon attaining the fruit.
By means of these three types of faith, one is able to destroy the obstacle of the icchantika’s lack of faith and enter the stage of the ten faiths;

therefore, it is called the "Great Meaning of Severing Doubt. The Master of the *Kosa* (Zangshi) said: "One who wishes to discuss the Great Dharma—'the Great Dharma' here refers to the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle.
Since we are now discussing the One Vehicle, one severs both the old and new doubts regarding the mind. The 'old doubt' refers to [doubts held] for over forty years..."
Every year, they would harbor this thought: "We have all entered the same Dharma-nature; why then does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Lesser Vehicle?
Those who newly gave rise to such doubts thought, "I now have doubts regarding my own wisdom;
perhaps I cannot yet fully comprehend whether this is the ultimate Dharma or merely the practice of the path. To sever these doubts, he now teaches the One Vehicle. This is...

Therefore, desiring to discuss the Great Dharma, secondly, one desires to rain down the great rain of the Dharma. How so? It is because the aspiration is to increase the great significance of the body of wisdom.
The Dharma flows from the Buddha; the rain is able to moisten the body of wisdom, thus serving as "rain. Since one has already attained faith, there must necessarily follow wisdom.
If the water of the Dharma does not rain down, then the body of wisdom will not arise. Therefore, next comes the raining down of the great rain of the Dharma, which increases [wisdom].

It increases the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*). At this time, one immediately breaks through the obstacles of the non-Buddhists' view of self and enters the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
Therefore, it is said that "the great significance of increasing the body of wisdom" is realized. Master Zang says:

"As for 'raining down the great rain of Dharma,' just as rain in the world can cause things to grow, so too does this rain of the Dharma of the One Vehicle moisten those of the three vehicles, causing them to enter the great wisdom of equality."
Śāriputra said: "Doubt and regret have been forever exhausted, for he dwells securely within the midst of true wisdom. This is the third striking of the great Dharma drum.
What is meant by "wishing to enter the profound realm of the śrāvakas"? "Striking" means to move. The "Dharma drum" refers to the sound of the Dharma.
It is called "profound" because it is the concentration that shatters space, which all śrāvakas and others are unable to hear.
The Tathāgata moves the sound of the Dharma so that it may be heard; this is called "entry.

By means of this power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that which is produced is as one wishes, like drawing objects out from empty space; hence it is named accordingly. At this time, the śrāvakas hear the sound of the Buddha-way.
Just as he rejoices in this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he immediately breaks through the obstacles of fear and suffering and enters the stage of the Ten Understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
This is called "entering the profound realm of the Śrāvaka. The Master of the *Pitaka* (Kuiji) says: "For those whose faculties are mature, there are two kinds of subtle and secret realms:

the third [stage] where one desires to beat the great Dharma drum, and the seventh [stage] where one desires the great Dharma drum. Since the preceding section has already clarified the Three Vehicles, [the following continues].
The body of wisdom is fully matured; now, desiring to bestow the prediction of Buddhahood upon those of the three vehicles, he speaks of the secret realm.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* causes those of the two vehicles to become Buddhas; it is called the "secret dharma" because it is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand.
Furthermore, for more than forty years, he had never clearly explained this matter, and thus it is termed "secret. This is the Great Dharma Drum.
These two phrases are a manifestation. "Because it is heard from afar" is the direct explanation of the name "Dharma Drum. Now, a drum causes its sound to be heard from afar;
here, by preaching the Great Dharma, it is universally bestowed upon those of the Three Vehicles, and this preaching is made to be heard from afar throughout the ten directions.
As for the manifestation of these two phrases: first, it is the striking of the Great Dharma Drum; second, it is the non-interruption of the Great Dharma Drum. Question: For what reason?
It is called the "Dharma that is never interrupted. The answer is: As for the Two Vehicles who seek solitary excellence, they certainly do not transmit the teaching through transformation.

However, if they receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, they will inevitably further transform others, causing them also to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, it is called the "Dharma drum that is never interrupted.
Master Jing says: Regarding the "uninterrupted great Dharma drum," how does it manifest the profound meaning of entering the secret realm of the Bodhisattvas?
This prediction causes the pratyekabuddhas to enter the secret realm of the bodhisattvas. The bodhisattva takes compassion as their essence;
to rescue beings from suffering without limit is their secret. As the Tathāgata’s Dharma-sound never ceases, they then enter the realm of compassion.

At this time, they break through the obstacle of self-attachment characteristic of the solitary realizers and enter the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Therefore, it is said that they "enter the great significance of the bodhisattvas’ secret realm."
Master Ki said: "Those who wish to beat the great Dharma drum hear the former Śrāvaka vehicle as the provisional and esoteric realm;

now, by revealing the Bodhisattva vehicle that has been taught, it is made the real and esoteric realm. This causes them to abandon their former provisional attachments and desire to return to the present reality;
thus, he beats the drum of these two. Regarding 'erecting the great Dharma banner amidst the five desires,' how does this manifest progress and attainment?"

The supreme and ultimate purity is the great meaning. A banner (*dhvaja*) has the characteristic of excelling and surpassing others. Within the first four stages (*bhūmi*), one attains the *samādhi* of the Mahāyāna Light;
because it can destroy darkness, it is called "light. Within these four stages, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is manifested, which is likened to a banner.

At this time, one destroys the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance in those who lack aspiration (*icchantika*), namely the *saṃskṛta-jarāmaraṇa* (death associated with conditioned effort), and enters the Great Purity.
Therefore, it is said that one "advances toward and attains the supreme, supreme purity and great meaning. The Master of the *Pitaka* (Kuiji) says:
"One who enters the secret realm is caused to advance toward and attain the supreme, supreme pure meaning" because this explains the desire to erect the great banner of the Dharma.

Once those of the Three Vehicles have received their predictions, they subsequently practice the bodhisattva path. The bodhisattva remains far removed from the two extremes; this is the practice of the Middle Way. Therefore...
It encompasses the supreme purity. Since the Dharma-banner is thus lofty, it encompasses the highest of the high. In the six desire realms, one kindles the great Dharma-lamp.
How does this manifest the great purpose of advancing toward the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)? Kindling the lamp has the characteristic of illuminating phenomena.
In the subsequent three stages, one attains the *Samādhi* of the King who Accumulates Merit; therein, all wholesome dharmas—excluding Prajñā—are [included].

It is called "merit" (*puṇya*). Because it can produce, increase, and perfect [virtue], it is called "accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*). Because it exercises mastery over that which is produced, increased, and perfected, it is called "king" (*rāja*).
Relying on this samādhi within the fifth stage, one gives rise to the five types of clear wisdom (*pañca-prajñā*) to comprehend the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

Relying on this samādhi within the sixth stage, *prajñā* manifests before one, enabling the comprehension of the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Relying on this samādhi within the seventh stage, one contemplates defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Purity is non-dual, for it merges the ultimate and the conventional; because the three illuminations are perfected, it is likened to a lamp.
At this time, one destroys the habitual tendencies of the heterodox view of self and enters the state of the Great Self within the cycle of dependent origination and birth-and-death;

therefore, it is said that one advances toward the great purpose of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Master Tsongkhapa said: "Those who wish to kindle the great lamp of the Dharma—now, a lamp has two meanings."

First, it destroys darkness; second, it reveals things. When the practice of those of the Three Vehicles is fulfilled, they destroy the darkness of ignorance and attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
thus, they are able to perceive dharmas such as the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). The preceding four phrases cause the causal practice of the Three Vehicles to be accomplished;
this present phrase causes the fruit-virtue of the Three Vehicles to be fulfilled. [The seventh point: The wind of desire blows the Great Dharma.
The Conch. How does it manifest the great meaning of the chapters, titles, and phrases? Blowing the conch is taken as the characteristic of changing the designation.
In the eighth and ninth stages, one attains the Samādhi of Worthy Protection (*bhadrapāla*). "Worthy" has two meanings: first, being able to dwell in manifest peace and happiness;
second, being able to attract and gather all merits. Within the eighth stage, by relying on this samādhi, one proceeds upon the single path.
In order to accomplish the Buddha-dharma, one relies on this samādhi within the ninth stage and proceeds upon the single path.

In order to bring sentient beings to accomplishment, once the single path of reality has been traversed, the designations of the three vehicles are consequently transformed. This is likened to blowing a conch shell;
at this time, the śrāvaka’s habitual tendency toward the fear of suffering is shattered, and one enters the state of great bliss within the realm of existence. Therefore, it is said:
Regarding the establishment of the names, phrases, and meanings of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and its great significance, the Master of the Piṭakas says:

"Blowing the great dharma-conch" refers to producing the sounds of speech. After those of the three vehicles have attained the fruit of Buddhahood, they further preach all the teachings for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, it is said that they establish the names, phrases, and sentences for all dharmas. Eighth, the desire to expound the Great Dharma.
What is the great meaning of manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma through realized wisdom? Turning the wheel has the characteristic of destroying obscurations.
In the tenth stage and the Buddha stage, one attains the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*. *Śūra* means "valiant" (*kṣānti*), and *aṅgama* means "to proceed."
Bodhisattvas and Buddhas possess four supreme virtues, and for this reason they are called "valiant" (*kṣānti*): first, fearlessness, because they have attained all-knowledge;
second, freedom from doubt, because they see that there is no one equal to themselves; third, solidity, because they always abide in contemplation without distraction.

It possesses four superior capacities: because it can shatter the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*) which is otherwise difficult to break; because a person endowed with the four virtues is able to practice this samādhi, it is called *gamana* (going);

and for one who attains this samādhi, their own practice becomes perfected, they extensively engage in benefiting others, they are able to destroy the habitual tendencies of self-love characteristic of the Pratyekabuddhas, and they immediately transcend birth and death to enter the state of Great Permanence. If one does not realize this...
This refers to being unable to explain the great meaning of turning the wheel of Dharma through the realization of the ineffable wisdom that leads others into it.
Based on these eight phrases, one causes those eight obstacles to enter the eight stages, thereby accomplishing the eight great benefits and the eight great meanings.
Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of the world of names, chapters, and sentences, which is the accomplishment of the profound cause," this is the explanation within the ten chapters.

Chapter Two: On the Scriptural Passages. Regarding the scriptural passages, the commentary intends to explain that they are the words of the sutra intended for all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
Question: For what reason is it said that the meaning of the names, chapters, and phrases is profoundly deep? Answer:
The teachings of the Three Vehicles conform to the worldly mind and do not aspire toward the ultimate reality; therefore, they are called "worldly."
"Names and phrases" refers to the names and phrases of the teachings of the Three Vehicles. "The meaning is profound" refers to the underlying intent of the Buddha’s teaching of the Three Vehicles;

therefore, it is said that the meaning is profound.
Regarding the third, the accomplishment of the cause of rare manifestation: there are four kinds of rarity. First, the difficulty of encountering [the teaching] at the right time;

second, the difficulty of encountering a person who can teach it; third, the difficulty of encountering the opportunity to hear the Dharma; and fourth, the difficulty of encountering a disciple capable of requesting it.
By means of these four, they are called "rare. "Inconceivable" means that it transcends the realm of emotional calculation. "Incomprehensible" means that it transcends the realm of verbal discussion.

"Immeasurable" (*aprameya*) means it is not an object that can be reached by analogy or calculation. As the present sutra says: "Infinite" (*amita*) means it transcends the portion of calculation and the portion of analogy;

"boundless" (*ananta*) means it transcends the portion of time; "inconceivable" (*acintya*) means it transcends the portion of intellectual deliberation. This is identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which transcends these four portions.
There are two kinds of eons (*kalpa*): first, an unspeakable eon, and second, an unspeakable time. [The eon is...]
Regarding that which can be expressed: one eon (*kalpa*) constitutes a single unit, continuing up to the "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*), which is termed an *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
Regarding time that cannot be expressed: as explained in this treatise, for the five kinds of eons, one night constitutes a single unit, continuing up to the incalculable.
Counting even up to a year as a single unit until reaching the "incalculable" (asaṃkhyeya), these are called the five kinds of kalpas.
Regarding the fourth point, the accomplishment of the visible, supreme, and wondrous causes, the Upādhyāya said: "Supreme and wondrous" refers to the twenty thousand Buddhas.
To receive and utilize the Lotus Sutra solely within one's own inner mind, without explaining it to others, is called "supremely sublime. Master Zang said:
"The teachings of the Three Vehicles spoken by twenty trillion Buddhas all possess the seven excellences; therefore, they are called 'supremely sublime.'"

Regarding the fifth, the accomplishment of the great cause of manifest enjoyment: when the Eight Princes and others were laymen, they enjoyed the exquisite pleasures of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
When they left the household life, for sixty minor *kalpas*, their bodies and minds remained unmoving as they enjoyed the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-sukha*).
Because that which was received was so vast, it is termed "great."

Sixth, regarding the "Manifest Perception that Encompasses the Achievement of All Buddhas Turning the Wheel of Dharma": the preceding five chapters have clarified the completion of the Buddha’s activities in transforming sentient beings;
the next four chapter-headings clarify his ability to benefit others; and the final one clarifies the benefits for those being transformed.
In this present chapter, it is explained how the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, harmonized the scriptures during the period of the Semblance Dharma.
This refers to the uninterrupted turning of the wheel of Dharma. As for the phrase "all Buddhas," it means that one perceives all Buddhas turning [the wheel] before oneself;
subsequently, after the Buddhas have passed into extinction, the Bodhisattva spreads it without ceasing, thereby ensuring that the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas remains uninterrupted.
For this reason, it is said to be "all."
Regarding the seventh [point], the accomplishment of the cause for the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma—which is directly perceived, virtuous, firm, and solid—it is as follows:
after eighty eons, the Bodhisattva *Prabhāsa* and the eight princes caused them to become firm in unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Because they taught the wheel of Dharma through unsurpassed *bodhi* over immeasurable time without it being destroyed, it is called the "virtuous, firm, and solid wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata."
The Wheel.

Among the seventeen names [of the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*] according to the treatise, it is the thirteenth name: *Sarvabuddhamahopāyakauśalyasūtra*.
Having attained great bodhi by relying on this dharma-gate, [the Buddha] preached for the sake of sentient beings the paths of humans, devas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
The dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas and others are called the "great skillful means" (mahopāya-kauśalya); therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (Upāya-paṭala).

Furthermore, because the subsequent treatise clarifies that the Buddha possesses seven kinds of skillful means, it is called the "Chapter on Skillful Means. According to the subsequent treatise, the author of the commentary (the Śāstrakāra) divides the "Skillful Means" into five parts:
first, he explains the merit of the sublime Dharma; next, he explains the merit of the Tathāgata as a Dharma-preacher. Second...
The third is the section on the three meanings of the great assembly; the fourth is the section on the four meanings of the Tathāgata;

and the fifth is the section explaining the four kinds of doubts. The Upādhyāya says: "The second [section] consists of five parts. It refutes duality to clarify unity and opens the gate of skillful means.
Although this chapter, from its beginning, primarily follows the true nature (dharmatā), it speaks of opening the gate of skillful means as its primary focus."
The passages that open up the provisional means are numerous, while the passages that reveal the true reality are concise.

Regarding the numerous passages that open up the provisional means, these refer to the eight types of Āgamas, as well as the fourfold explanations concerning the merits of the Dharma Master and so forth. As for the concise passages that reveal the true reality:
This is because it exclusively takes up the texts concerning the Buddhas' wisdom, which is profoundly deep and immeasurable.

Regarding the refutation of duality and the elucidation of unity, there are three different explanations. The first states: "Refuting duality" means refuting the attachments of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha);

"elucidating unity" refers precisely to the bodhisattva vehicle. The second explanation states: "Refuting duality" refers to the two categories of the Great and Small Vehicles, with the two vehicles combined as one.
One category refers to the Bodhisattva vehicle as one category. Because these two attachments are destroyed, it is said that "the two are destroyed.

To clarify "one" means the ten kinds of unsurpassed [qualities] as explained in the third [chapter]. The two vehicles are combined into one category, and the two types of bodhisattvas are combined into one category;
namely, the Bodhisattva vehicle within the Three Vehicles, and the bodhisattvas who are the objects of the "cloud and rain" [teaching] which is to be remedied.
These are combined into a single category. To refute these two, it is said that "the two are refuted. To clarify "the one," there are ten kinds of unsurpassed [qualities]:
the section praising the Dharma identifies and takes up "the one"; the section praising the Teacher indicates the person who is able to preach; and the section of inquiry and request [is included].
This reveals the three vehicles through the section on "Revealing the Refutation" (*prabheda*). The section on "Bestowing Prophecies" (*vyākaraṇa*) manifests the single path capable of refutation.

The section on "Severing Doubts" (*saṃśayacchedana*) further definitively establishes the time and place, universally clarifying the methods of transmission and reception; that is to say, two kinds of methods: first, the method of relinquishing (*utsarga*), and second, the method of opening (*apavāda*).
